title: Reconnaissance
summary: Reconnaissance is the set of adversary activities that gather information about a target before and alongside intrusion attempts, and it is the one tactic where most of the work can happen entirely outside the victim's visibility. Attackers enumerate publicly reachable services, harvest employee names and email addresses from social media and conference sites, fingerprint technology stacks from HTTP responses and TLS certificates, review job postings for named products, and search breach data and code repositories for credentials that were never meant to be public. Active variants cross into the target's own address space: port and service scanning, directory brute forcing, DNS zone transfer attempts, and probing of VPN or webmail portals that leave firewall, load balancer, and web server logs. Telemetry available to defenders is thin and noisy. Internet-facing sensors, honeypots, passive DNS, certificate transparency monitoring, and brand monitoring can reveal scanning or credential-harvesting infrastructure, while email security gateways may show early directory-harvest attempts or spoofed display names. Detection is difficult in isolation because scanning traffic is indistinguishable from vulnerability scanners, search engine crawlers, and researchers on most networks, and because the highest-value reconnaissance often produces no packets to the target at all. Effective defence is therefore mostly preparation: reducing the public attack surface, keeping an accurate external asset inventory, monitoring certificate and DNS changes, and correlating low-severity internet telemetry so the earliest stage of a campaign is not silently discarded.
objectives: Explain how the Reconnaissance tactic maps to adversary information gathering before initial access, and why most of it never touches victim-owned infrastructure.

Identify the telemetry that genuinely exists for this tactic: internet-facing scan logs, honeypot hits, passive DNS, certificate transparency records, email gateway anomalies, and brand monitoring feeds.
Distinguish opportunistic scanning noise from targeted enumeration using source reputation, timing, target selection, and request content.
Correlate several low-severity external observations, such as certificate issuance for a lookalike domain plus a login-attempt spike, into one campaign hypothesis.
Assess how much of an estate is discoverable from the public internet and prioritise attack-surface reduction accordingly.
Write and tune triage logic that suppresses crawler and vulnerability-scanner noise without discarding targeted probing.

beginner.definition: Reconnaissance is the research an attacker does before touching your systems. They look for staff email addresses, exposed services and technology details. Most of this can be done from public information, so nothing appears in your logs. Only the active probing reaches your network.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers rarely guess. They check first, and that is why a well-researched attack succeeds. If you know what is visible about you, you can shrink that surface. You cannot block research, but you can remove easy clues. Fewer exposed services mean fewer doors to try, and fewer public details mean more convincing mistakes from the attacker.
howItWorks: The attacker reads public sources, such as your website and staff profiles on social media.
They collect email addresses and note the names of tools your job adverts mention.
They check which of your services answer directly from the public internet.
Then they probe those services directly, looking for versions with known weaknesses.
Defenders see this probing in firewall records, which log network traffic, mixed with constant background noise.
beginner.example: Think of a thief choosing a house. They walk past on different days, note when the lights go out, and check which windows face away from the street. They may look at the name on the letterbox. None of this touches the house, so no alarm rings. The actual break-in comes much later. Reconnaissance is that quiet walk past, and it is why a good lock and fewer visible clues matter.
takeaways: Reconnaissance is research, and most of it never touches your network.
Know what is publicly visible about your company and your staff.
Active probing does show up, so watch your internet-facing logs closely.
